sermon:
## Fan Into Flame
*A dying man writes a frightened one and tells him to stop hiding the fire*

**Text:** 2 Timothy 1:1-18 · **Supporting:** Romans 1:16; 1 Corinthians 4:17; Acts 16:1-3; Hebrews 2:14-15

This is the last letter Paul ever wrote, and he wrote it to a man who was losing his nerve. Not losing his faith. Losing his nerve. There is a difference, and most of us live in the gap between the two. Timothy still believed. He had been raised in the Scriptures by a grandmother named Lois and a mother named Eunice; Paul had ordained him with his own hands. The gift was real. And it was going out, like a coal left at the edge of the fire, still red but cooling, and the apostle in chains can see it from across the empire.

**The gift was real and the fire was dying**
"Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands." (2 Timothy 1:6) The word translated stir up is the word for rekindling a banked fire — to fan the coal back into flame. Paul does not tell Timothy to go get more of the Spirit. He tells him to rekindle what he already has. We have inverted this. We treat spiritual coldness as a supply problem, as though God has been stingy and the answer is a better conference, a fresh experience, a new anointing. Paul treats it as a tending problem. The fire was given. The fire is going out. And the going-out has a name, and Paul names it in the next breath: "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind." (2 Timothy 1:7) Fear was banking the coal. Fear always does. Fear does not announce itself as fear — it dresses up as prudence, as caution, as waiting for the right moment, as not wanting to make things worse. Timothy was not a coward. He was a careful young pastor in a hostile city watching his mentor get arrested for the very message he was supposed to preach, and the careful thing, the wise-seeming thing, was to lower the flame. Paul will not allow it. Power, love, a sound mind — that is the Spirit you were given. Not the other one.

**Stop being ashamed of a chained man**
Then Paul says the thing that costs him to say it. "Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner." (2 Timothy 1:8) He knows what he is asking. He is a convict. Association with him is dangerous, and he has watched men do the arithmetic and walk away — "all they which are in Asia be turned away from me," he writes near the end of the letter. He knew the pull to be embarrassed by a gospel that lands you in a cell, because he had spent his life refusing it. "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ," he had told the Romans years before, "for it is the power of God unto salvation" (Romans 1:16). The same word. He is asking Timothy to share his own long, hard-won unembarrassment.

And notice what he does not appeal to. He does not appeal to Timothy's record, his gifting, his promise. He appeals to God's prior act: God "hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began." (2 Timothy 1:9) Before the world began. The cure for a fading fire is not to look at the size of your flame. It is to look at the age of the purpose that lit it. You were chosen before there was a world to be ashamed in front of.

**What we are really guarding**
Here is where I have to climb inside the indictment, because I have done the careful, fire-lowering thing and called it discernment. I have softened a sermon because of who was in the room. I have let a coal cool and told myself I was being strategic. The shame Paul is naming is not the shame of denying Christ outright. It is the quieter shame that just turns the heat down, that keeps the faith but keeps it manageable, that guards the reputation instead of the deposit. And Paul's word for what Timothy is to keep is exactly that — a deposit. "That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us." (2 Timothy 1:14) Not your gift. Not your platform. The deposit. The gospel itself, handed to you to be handed on intact, and you do not have the authority to dilute it to make it safer to carry.

Why can a chained man speak this way about a fire and a deposit and not flinch at the executioner outside his door? Because of one sentence buried in the next chapter that governs this whole letter: Christ "hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel" (2 Timothy 1:10). Abolished. The thing Timothy was lowering his flame to avoid, the thing fear bows to, the thing that made Paul's chains a credible threat — Christ went through it and broke it from the inside. The writer of Hebrews says He did it precisely "that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil; and deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage" (Hebrews 2:14-15). All their lifetime, subject to bondage, through fear. That is the chain under Timothy's caution. That is the chain under mine. And it is the one chain Christ already struck off. Paul is in a Roman cell asking a frightened young man to live as though the worst thing has already lost — because for the man in the cell, it has.

The one who calls you to fan the flame already walked into the fire that should have consumed you and came out carrying the keys.

Guard the deposit. Stop being ashamed.

## Soldier, Athlete, Farmer
*Three pictures of a man who refuses to make the gospel easy on himself*

**Text:** 2 Timothy 2:1-26 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 9:24-27; Ephesians 6:11-13; John 12:24; Acts 14:22

We want a Christianity that costs us nothing and changes everything. Paul knew that hunger and refused to feed it. From a cell, with the sword already in view, he hands his successor not a strategy for comfort but three pictures of strain, and he picks the three hardest working men in the ancient world to do it. A soldier. An athlete. A farmer. None of them is having an easy day. Every one of them is doing something difficult on purpose, and that is the point.

**Grace is not the absence of hardship**
The chapter opens where every chapter Paul writes opens: "Thou therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus." (2 Timothy 2:1) Be strong in grace. We have so domesticated that word that it sounds like a synonym for going easy. Paul means the opposite. Grace is the power that strengthens a man for the hardship he does not avoid. It is not the thing that gets him out of the fight; it is the thing that holds him in it. "Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ." (2 Timothy 2:3) And then the first picture turns on a single, surgical line: "No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier." (2 Timothy 2:4) Entangle. The soldier's danger is not the enemy in front of him. It is the small civilian comforts behind him that slowly attach themselves to him until he cannot move. Paul, who told the Ephesians to "put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil" (Ephesians 6:11), knew that the wiles are rarely a frontal assault. They are entanglements. A thousand reasonable attachments that leave a soldier unable to march when the order comes.

**Win by the rules, eat from your own labor**
The second picture is the athlete, and it has a catch. "And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully." (2 Timothy 2:5) You can run hard and still be disqualified. Effort is not enough; the effort has to be lawful, run inside the lines God drew. Paul had used this same picture on the Corinthians, telling them he beat his own body into submission "lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway" (1 Corinthians 9:27). The man with the most platform is not exempt from the rules of the race. He is more accountable to them. And then the third picture, the slowest one: "The husbandman that laboureth must be first partaker of the fruits." (2 Timothy 2:6) The farmer eats first — but only the laboring farmer. There is no fruit without the long, unglamorous, sun-up work in the dirt that no one applauds. Soldier, athlete, farmer. Discipline, lawfulness, labor. Not one of them describes a comfortable man.

**The word is not chained, and neither is the future of it**
Then Paul says the line that the whole letter leans on. He is the soldier, and he is losing. "Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound." (2 Timothy 2:9) They have him. They do not have the word. The chain on Paul's wrist cannot reach the message, and Paul knows it, and that knowledge is what lets him keep handing the future to other people from inside a place with no future for himself. Which is exactly what he does: "And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also." (2 Timothy 2:2) Count the generations in that one verse. Paul, to Timothy, to faithful men, to others also. Four links, and Paul can see only the first one of them, and he sets the whole chain in motion anyway from a cell he will not leave alive.

I have to stop here and confess the version of ministry I am tempted by, because it is the opposite of this. I am tempted to gather, not to entrust. To be the indispensable one, the link the chain runs through, rather than the man who pours himself into faithful people and then gets out of the way. Entrusting the gospel to others means trusting that it does not finally depend on me — and something in me does not want that to be true. Paul wanted it to be true. Paul was dying to make it true.

**The grain that will not rise unless it dies**
Under all three pictures is one law that Christ said about Himself first. "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." (John 12:24) The soldier, the athlete, the farmer — each of them is a small picture of that one law: nothing lives until something dies. Paul is the grain of wheat falling into the Roman ground, and he is not panicking, because he has watched it work once already. Christ fell into the ground. Christ did not abide alone. The empty tomb is the harvest of that buried seed, and Paul, going down into the same ground, is counting on the same God who raised the first grain. "It is a faithful saying: For if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him." (2 Timothy 2:11) That is why a chained man can be this calm about the chain. He knows what God does with buried things.

Endure. Entrust it to faithful men.

## When the Last Days Are Hard
*What to hold onto when the form of godliness has lost its power*

**Text:** 2 Timothy 3:1-17 · **Supporting:** Matthew 24:12; Romans 1:21-25; 2 Peter 1:20-21; Psalm 119:105

Paul does not tell Timothy the last days will be easy. He tells him they will be hard, and then he tells him why, and the why is not what we expect. We brace for persecution from outside, for the lions and the swords and the empire. Paul looks past all of that and points at something happening inside the room. "This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come." (2 Timothy 3:1) Perilous — the word is used one other time in the New Testament, for a man so violent no one could pass that way. The danger Paul sees is not coming for the church from the outside. It is a danger you have to walk through to get anywhere, and it wears the clothes of religion.

**A catalog that begins and ends with love aimed wrong**
Then comes one of the most unsparing lists in Scripture, and it is worth hearing the shape of it. "For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy." (2 Timothy 3:2) Notice where it starts and where it lands. It opens with lovers of their own selves and closes, a verse later, with "lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God." (2 Timothy 3:4) The whole catalog is bracketed by disordered love. These are not people who stopped loving. They are people whose love came home to roost on themselves. Paul had already diagnosed this in Romans, where men "changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator" (Romans 1:25). The peril of the last days is not that love grows cold in the abstract. It is that love turns inward and curdles. And then Paul lands the indictment on the one place we would have thought was safe: "Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away." (2 Timothy 3:5)

**The form is intact and the power is gone**
Sit with that combination, because it is the most dangerous one in the chapter. A form of godliness. Not the absence of religion — the presence of it, hollowed out. The shape is there. The vocabulary is there. The services run, the words are right, and the power is gone. Jesus had warned of the same thing: "because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold" (Matthew 24:12) — and He said it not of pagans but of His own. A form denying its own power is more dangerous than open unbelief, because open unbelief at least knows it is empty. The form does not. It can go on for years convinced it is full.

And I will not pretend I am only the diagnostician here, because I have led services that had the form and were begging God for the power, and I have not always been able to tell from the inside which kind of day it was. That is the terror of this verse. You cannot reliably feel the difference between a full form and an empty one while you are standing inside it. The form feels the same either way. Paul is not describing a far-off apostate church. He is describing a temptation that runs straight through the middle of every faithful pastor and every faithful congregation, and the only safety is to keep checking the form against the power and never assume the power because you still have the form.

**Two anchors against the drift**
So what holds Timothy when the form is everywhere and the power is rare? Paul gives him two anchors, and the first one is people. "But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them." (2 Timothy 3:14) Of whom. Not just what you learned, but from whom — Lois, Eunice, Paul himself, faces with names, people whose lives backed up their words. Faith is handed down through trustworthy people, and Timothy is to remember the ones whose godliness had power in it.

The second anchor is older and steadier than any person. "And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus." (2 Timothy 3:15) And then the verse the whole church has built on: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: that the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works." (2 Timothy 3:16-17) Given by inspiration of God — breathed out by God. When the form is everywhere and the power has leaked out of it, here is a word that did not come from men and cannot be hollowed out by men. Peter says the same: the prophecy "came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost" (2 Peter 1:21). The form fails because it is ours. The Scripture holds because it is His breath.

**The breath that makes a man complete**
Why does a God-breathed Scripture make the man of God complete when his own form of godliness cannot? Because the Scripture does not point at itself. It is "able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus" — it carries you to the one who is the power the form had lost. The same Christ who abolished death stands at the center of the writings Timothy had known since childhood, and it is union with Him, not the intactness of our religious shape, that furnishes a man for every good work. The word is breathed out by God precisely so that when everything human about our godliness fails the power test, there is one thing in the room that never came from us and never loses its power.

Scripture is God-breathed. Continue in it.

## Preach the Word, Finish the Race
*The last charge of a man who can already see the finish line*

**Text:** 2 Timothy 4:1-22 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 9:24-26; Philippians 3:13-14; Acts 20:24; Revelation 2:10

These are the last recorded words of the apostle Paul. Not a memoir, not a defense, not a settling of accounts. A charge. A man who knows the sword is coming uses his final breath to hand the next preacher his marching orders, and the orders are aimed straight past Timothy at every one of us who has ever stood up to speak for God and felt the pull to say something easier. "I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom." (2 Timothy 4:1) He swears Timothy in. This is not advice. This is an oath taken before the Judge.

**Preach it whether it lands or not**
"Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine." (2 Timothy 4:2) In season and out of season — when it is welcome and when it is not, when it fills the room and when it empties it. Paul does not tell Timothy to read the room and adjust the message. He tells him the message does not move with the room. And he tells him exactly why the temptation to move it will become unbearable: "For the time will come when they will not endure sound teaching; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears." (2 Timothy 4:3) Heap to themselves teachers. They will assemble a faculty of voices that tell them what they already want, and there will always be men willing to be hired for it. The itching ear is not a market Timothy is to serve. It is a sickness he is to refuse to scratch.

I have to be honest about which side of that verse is the more tempting one for a preacher. It is not the itching ear in the pew. It is the willing teacher in the pulpit. I know the pull to scratch the itch, to give the room the word it came hoping to hear, to mistake a full house for a faithful one. Paul's charge is brutal precisely here. "Watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry." (2 Timothy 4:5) Endure afflictions — because preaching the unwelcome word in an itching-ear age is an affliction, and Paul will not pretend otherwise.

**A man looking at his own death without flinching**
Then the letter turns, and it turns to the man holding the pen. "For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand." (2 Timothy 4:6) Ready to be offered — the word for a drink-offering poured out at the base of the altar, the last of the wine emptied onto the ground. Paul is not facing death. He is pouring himself out into it, on purpose, the way the farmer's seed went into the ground, the way the grain fell. And then the line that men have wanted on their lips at the end ever since: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." (2 Timothy 4:7) Listen to the three. The soldier from chapter two — I have fought. The athlete — I have finished my course. The farmer who kept the deposit — I have kept the faith. The whole letter compresses into one sentence at the end of a life. Years earlier he had told the Ephesian elders he wanted only to "finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 20:24). Now the course is finished. He made it.

And then he tells us how he is so sure of the verdict, and it is not by pointing at his record. "Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day." (2 Timothy 4:8) Laid up — set aside, reserved, already secured before the trial. The crown is not the wage Paul earned by fighting well. It is the gift the righteous Judge gives, and Paul tells us who else gets it in the same breath: "and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing." (2 Timothy 4:8) Not the heroic. Not the apostles. All who love His appearing. The crown is not a reward for a record like Paul's. It is the inheritance of everyone who loved the One who is coming.

**The faithful One when the man fails**
We would like to read "I have kept the faith" as the boast of a man who never wavered, and then the rest of the chapter takes the boast apart. "Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world." "At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me." (2 Timothy 4:10, 16) This is not a triumphant scene. This is a cold cell, a man asking for his cloak and his books, abandoned by his friends, writing in the dark. And from inside that abandonment he says, "Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me." (2 Timothy 4:17) The crown is laid up not because Paul kept everything but because Christ kept Paul. The same letter said it plainly two chapters back: "if we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself" (2 Timothy 2:13). That is the only ground a dying man has under him. Not his fight, not his course, not even his faith — but a Judge who is also the One who poured Himself out first, who abolished death and went ahead through it to hold the crown on the other side.

The finish line is not a wage you earn. It is a Person who already crossed it and turned around to wait for you.

I have kept the faith. Preach.
